cards.headline: The borrower changes everything.
cards.body: Every bond is a loan, but who you lend to sets the risk and the reward. A national government, a blue-chip company, and a struggling one all borrow — and a lender demands a very different rate from each.

art.alt: Three lenders notes rise on steps — a solid vault with a short flag, a firm building taller, a cracked building with the tallest — more reward as the borrower looks shakier.

cards.headline: Government bonds: the safe end.
cards.body: A stable government that borrows in its own currency is the safest kind of borrower, because it is highly unlikely to miss a payment. In return for that safety, these bonds pay the lowest interest. Safety and yield trade off.

cards.headline: Corporate bonds: paid for risk.
cards.body: Companies borrow too, and they can fail in ways a government usually cannot. To make up for that added default risk, corporate bonds pay a higher coupon. The weaker the company, the higher the rate it must offer.

cards.headline: Municipal bonds: the tax angle.
cards.body: Cities and states issue bonds to fund roads, schools and water. In many places the interest carries a tax break, so a lower coupon can still leave more in your pocket than a higher, fully taxed one. Compare after tax.

cards.headline: Ratings grade the risk.
cards.body: Agencies grade borrowers from top-tier down to speculative. High grades mean safer, lower-paying bonds; low grades — 'high-yield' or 'junk' — pay more precisely because they might not pay at all. The rating is shorthand for default risk.

cards.prompt: Two bonds, same maturity: one from a stable government, one from a shaky company. Which pays the higher coupon?
cards.explanation: A riskier borrower has to offer more to attract lenders. The higher coupon is not a free bonus — it is compensation for a real chance the money is not paid back. More yield always marks more risk.

cards.title: Yield rises with risk
cards.caption: Yield climbs with risk: safest government debt pays least, speculative 'high-yield' pays most. The extra percentage points are the market's price for a chance of default.

cards.body: A lower credit rating signals a greater chance of default, so those bonds must pay a [[1]] coupon to attract lenders.
cards.explanation: Risk and reward move together in bonds. A weaker borrower can only compete for lenders by paying more — which is why a fat yield is a warning as much as an attraction.

cards.summary: Bonds differ by who issues them, and yield always rises with the borrower's risk of default.
bullets: Government bonds are safest and pay the least.
Corporate and high-yield bonds pay more for more risk.
Credit ratings are a shorthand for default risk.

art.alt: Three lenders notes rise on steps — a solid vault with a short flag, a firm building taller, a cracked building with the tallest — more reward as the borrower looks shakier.

cards.insight: In bonds, a higher yield is never a gift. It is the exact measure of how worried the market is about being repaid.
